subject: ophthalmology
title: Lens and cataract

steps.tx: Age-related **senile cataract** represents the leading cause of reversible visual impairment worldwide. Cortical cataracts cause spoke opacities with glare and monocular polyopia. Nuclear cataracts demonstrate amber brunescence with an index myopic shift that transiently improves reading, known as second sight. Posterior subcapsular opacities form granular plaques along the visual axis, degrading daytime vision in diabetics and steroid users. Morgagnian progression liquefies the cortex, allowing the dense brown nucleus to sink inferiorly and risking phacolytic glaucoma.
steps.say: Age related senile cataract is the most common cause of reversible visual impairment in elderly patients. Cortical cataracts cause spoke opacities that produce significant glare and multiple images. Nuclear sclerosis produces brownish discolouration of the lens and induces a myopic shift, giving patients temporary second sight for reading. Posterior subcapsular opacities form along the visual axis, creating disabling daytime glare. Untreated mature cataracts can liquefy their cortical material, predisposing the eye to severe inflammatory phacolytic glaucoma.

steps.tx: Early detection of **congenital cataract** is vital to prevent stimulus-deprivation amblyopia in infants, presenting with leukocoria or an absent red reflex on newborn screening. Unilateral cataracts usually stem from trauma, persistent fetal vasculature or local dysgenesis. Bilateral cataracts suggest intrauterine infections such as rubella, metabolic disorders like galactosaemia with oil-drop opacities, or Down syndrome. Dense bilateral cataracts require lensectomy and anterior vitrectomy within six to eight weeks of life, followed by immediate optical correction and patching.
steps.say: Early recognition of congenital cataract is crucial to prevent profound amblyopia in infants. A white pupil or absent red reflex on Bruckner screening mandates immediate ophthalmological assessment. Bilateral cases often indicate maternal rubella with salt and pepper retinopathy, metabolic disorders like galactosaemia, or Down syndrome. Unilateral opacities usually follow persistent fetal vasculature or local dysgenesis. Dense bilateral cataracts require surgical lensectomy and anterior vitrectomy within eight weeks of birth, accompanied by prompt optical correction and diligent patching therapy.

steps.tx: The standard surgical intervention for cataract is **phacoemulsification**, performed through a small self-sealing corneal incision under topical anesthesia. Continuous curvilinear capsulorhexis allows ultrasonic fragmentation and aspiration of the nucleus, followed by in-the-bag implantation of a foldable intraocular lens. Optical biometry calculates target lens power using axial length and keratometry. Manual small-incision surgery serves very dense brown cataracts where excessive ultrasound risks endothelial burn. Capsular tension rings provide equatorial stability when zonular weakness complicates pseudoexfoliation syndrome.
steps.say: Phacoemulsification is the primary surgical technique used to remove clouded lens material through micro incisions. The surgeon creates a continuous circular opening in the anterior capsule, emulsifies the hard nuclear core with ultrasound energy, and removes cortical remnants by irrigation. A flexible intraocular lens is then unfolded directly into the capsular bag. For very dense brunescent lenses, manual small incision surgery helps protect the corneal endothelium from thermal injury. When zonular support is weakened by pseudoexfoliation, inserting a capsular tension ring maintains stability.

steps.tx: Surveillance focuses on detecting postoperative **endophthalmitis**, typically presenting within the first week with severe ocular pain, red eye, hypopyon and vitritis. Immediate management requires vitreous tap and intravitreal injection of vancomycin and ceftazidime. Intraoperative posterior capsule rupture necessitates anterior vitrectomy to clear prolapsed vitreous. Posterior capsular opacification is the commonest late complication, caused by retained lens epithelial cells proliferating across the visual axis, which is cleared outpatient by neodymium YAG laser capsulotomy.
steps.say: Acute postoperative endophthalmitis is a vision threatening emergency that typically presents within a few days of surgery. Patients develop worsening ocular pain, marked redness, diminished vision and a layered hypopyon in the anterior chamber. Prompt vitreous aspiration and empirical intravitreal injections of vancomycin and ceftazidime are required to control the infection. Posterior capsular opacification is the most common late complication, which is easily cleared by an outpatient neodymium YAG laser capsulotomy to restore sharp vision.
